working: The shared condition is \(|z_1+z_2|^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2\). Expanding the left side gives \(|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2+2\operatorname{Re}(z_1\bar z_2)\), so \(\operatorname{Re}(z_1\bar z_2)=0\), i.e. \(z_1\bar z_2\) is purely imaginary. Check: \(z_1=1, z_2=i\) satisfies \(|1+i|^2=2=1+1\) and \(z_1\bar z_2=-i\), purely imaginary.

working: From Q2, \(z_1/z_2 = ik\) with \(k\) real. Then \(i(z_1/z_2) = i\cdot ik = -k\), a real number. For \(k<0\) the value \(-k\) is positive real, whose argument is 0; so 0 is a possible argument. working: Double the second equation: \(2x^2+4x+6\lambda=0\); subtract \(2x^2+3x+5\lambda=0\) to get \(x+\lambda=0\), so the common root is \(x=-\lambda\). Substituting into \(x^2+2x+3\lambda=0\) gives \(\lambda^2+\lambda=0\), so \(\lambda=0\) or \(\lambda=-1\). Both verify: \(\lambda=0\) shares root 0; \(\lambda=-1\) shares root 1 (\(2+3-5=0\), \(1+2-3=0\)).
Root 2 in \(x^2+\lambda x-12=0\) gives \(4+2\lambda-12=0\), so \(\lambda=4\). Equal roots in \(x^2+4x+\mu=0\) needs \(16-4\mu=0\), so \(\mu=4\). Hence \((\lambda,\mu)=(4,4)\).

working: Let \(f(x)=(x-a)(x-c)+2(x-b)(x-d)\), leading coefficient \(3>0\). With \(a<b<c<d\): \(f(b)=(b-a)(b-c)<0\) (positive times negative) and \(f(d)=(d-a)(d-c)>0\), so \(f\) changes sign and, being an upward parabola taking a negative value, has two distinct real roots. Numeric check \(a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3\): \(3x^2-10x+6=0\), discriminant \(100-72=28>0\).

Choosing 11 from 13 means excluding exactly 2 players, so at most 2 of the 4 bowlers can be left out and the team always contains at least \(4-2=2\) bowlers. Hence every selection qualifies: \(\binom{13}{11}=\binom{13}{2}=78\). (Confirmed by complement: 0-bowler teams need 11 from 9 non-bowlers = 0; 1-bowler teams need 10 from 9 = 0.)
No three points on a circle are collinear, so every choice of 3 of the 4 points forms a triangle: \(\binom{4}{3}=4\).
General term \(T_{r+1} = \binom{12}{r}(2x^2)^{12-r}(-1/x)^r\), whose \(x\)-power is \(2(12-r)-r = 24-3r\). Setting \(24-3r=0\) gives \(r=8\), so it is the \((r+1)=9\)th term.

working: Reading the intended condition as 'the coefficients of the \(p\)th and \(q\)th terms of \((1+x)^n\) are equal': \(\binom{n}{p-1} = \binom{n}{q-1}\) forces \((p-1)+(q-1)=n\), so \(p+q = n+2\). The same value follows from the adjacent-term reading printed here: if the \(p\)th and \((p+1)\)th coefficients are equal then \((p-1)+p=n\), so \(n=2p-1\) and \(p+(p+1)=2p+1=n+2\).

working: The six digits sum to 15, so omitting digit \(d\) leaves sum \(15-d\), divisible by 3 only for \(d\in\{0,3\}\). Omitting 0: digits \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) give \(5!=120\) numbers. Omitting 3: digits \(\{0,1,2,4,5\}\) give \(5!-4!=120-24=96\) (subtracting those with leading 0). Total \(120+96=216\).

Written homogeneously the system is \(x-cy-bz=0,\; -cx+y-az=0,\; -bx-ay+z=0\); a non-trivial solution requires the determinant of \([[1,-c,-b],[-c,1,-a],[-b,-a,1]]\) to vanish. Expanding gives \(1-a^2-b^2-c^2-2abc=0\), so \(a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc=1\). Numeric check \(a=1,b=c=0\): the system becomes \(x=0,\,y=z,\,z=y\), which has non-trivial solutions, and \(1+0+0+0=1\).
